newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh to sign peace deal with rebels shortly.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh to sign peace deal with rebels shortly.

text.p: Bangladesh on Wednesday said it had reached agreement with tribal leaders to end a decades-old insurgency in southeastern Chittagong Hill Tracts and would sign a peace deal soon.
"We have reached consensus on all issues. We are going to sign a peace deal very soon," chief government negotiator Abul Hasanat Abdullah told reporters in Dhaka.
Abdullah declined to say when the peace treaty between the government and tribal Shanti Bahini guerrillas would be signed or what it would contain.

But Kalparanjan Chakma, a member of the government negotiating team, told reporters the deal was expected to be signed after Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina had been briefed on the outcome of the four days of talks.
Hasina was due to return from a meeting of South Asian leaders in the Maldives on Wednesday night.
More than 500 civilians, rebels and soldiers have been killed in the insurgency started by the Shanti Bahini in 1973 over demands for autonomy of the Hill Tracts, bordering India and Burma.
The current round of peace talks is the fourth since Hasina took office in June last year.
Chakma said the tribal delegation would leave Dhaka in a day or two, indicating the deal would be sealed before they depart.

Abdullah, parliamentary chief whip of the ruiling Awami League, headed the government side at the talks. The rebel side was headed by Jyotirindra Budhipriya Larma, chief of the Shanti Bahini's political wing.
The rebels had insisted that some 500,000 Bengali-speaking settlers be expelled from the 5,500 square-mile (14,200 sq-km) Hill Tracts and the army be withdrawn.
How contentious issues weere solved was not immediately known.
The government has already started reclaiming tribal land and restoring it to thousands of tribal refugees who returned home in the first phase of a repatriation programme in March and April.
But the government had been refusing to expel Bengalis or pull out the troops from the region, fearing a backlash.
